lines.text: Do you know how hiccups work? It's your breathing muscle twitching, and your throat slamming shut.
Under your lungs is a dome-shaped muscle called the diaphragm. Normally it pulls down smoothly, and you breathe in.
In a hiccup, it suddenly jerks down on its own, and air rushes in.
A split second later, your vocal cords snap shut and stop the air. That snap is the hic.
It's often set off by eating too fast, fizzy drinks, or swallowed air, which bother the nerves that run the diaphragm.
Scientists think it's an ancient reflex. Babies even hiccup in the womb, long before they ever breathe air.
Most bouts stop within minutes. But one man, Charles Osborne, hiccuped on and off for sixty-eight years.
